title: Correlation isn't causation
summary: You can read a scatter plot. Learn the three questions that tell you whether two things that move together are cause and effect.
objective: Given a correlation, name a plausible confounder or reverse cause, and say what evidence would support a causal claim.
subject: data

hook.prompt: Hypothetical monthly data: ice cream sales and drownings rise and fall together. What's the most likely reason?

visual.alt: Scatter plot of monthly ice cream sales against drownings, rising together.

options.text: Eating ice cream before swimming causes cramps
options.feedback: That's the folk explanation, and there's no good evidence for it. Look for something that drives *both* numbers.

options.text: Something else pushes both numbers up
A coincidence in this dataset
options.feedback: Coincidences happen in small samples, but this pattern repeats every summer, so something real links them.

hook.explanation: Hot weather. More people swim and more people buy ice cream; neither causes the other. That hidden third thing is where this lesson starts.

katas.title: Confounders: a third thing drives both
katas.body: A **confounder** is a variable that affects both of the things you measured. Hot days push up ice cream sales *and* the number of people swimming, so sales and drownings move together even though neither causes the other. Before you read a correlation as cause, ask: **what else could move both?** If you can name one, the correlation alone can't settle it.

visual.alt: Scatter plot of ice cream sales against drownings; hot months cluster high on both axes and cool months low on both.

katas.prompt: Among children aged 5 to 12, shoe size correlates with reading score. Which confounder explains it?

options.text: Age
Family income
options.feedback: Income might affect reading, but it doesn't make feet bigger. A confounder has to move both variables.

options.text: Reading practice makes children grow
options.feedback: That's a causal story in the other direction, with no mechanism. Look for something that grows along with both feet and reading.

options.text: School quality
options.feedback: Same problem as income: it could affect reading, not shoe size.

katas.hint: What changes between age 5 and age 12 besides reading?
katas.explanation: Older children have bigger feet and read better. Compare children of the same age and the shoe-size correlation disappears.

katas.prompt: This chart card is from a hypothetical survey. Tap the part that claims more than the data shows.

visual.html:
Weekly exercise hours vs anxiety score

Hypothetical survey, 300 adults, one week

r = −0.6

Exercise cuts anxiety by a third

katas.hint: Which part would still be true if anxious people simply exercise less?
katas.explanation: The title, r value, and trend line describe the data. The caption turns a correlation into a causal claim; anxious people may exercise less, or free time may drive both.

katas.title: Which way does the arrow point?
katas.body: A correlation doesn't say which variable moves first. Cities with more police officers often have more crime. Police causing crime is unlikely; crime leading cities to hire police is not. This is **reverse causation**: the supposed effect is driving the supposed cause. Ask it every time: *could Y be causing X instead?* Time order helps: a cause can't come after its effect.

visual.alt: Two boxes, Police and Crime, with an arrow pointing each way between them.
visual.html: More police→ ?? ←More crime

katas.prompt: A hypothetical streaming app finds that users who tap *Skip intro* watch more episodes per week. The PM wants to enlarge the button to boost watching. What's the strongest objection?

options.text: Heavy watching may cause the tapping, not the reverse
The sample may be too small to show a real effect
options.feedback: A streaming app has plenty of users; the correlation is probably real. The problem is what it means, not how reliable it is.

options.text: The link could be a coincidence that fades with time
options.feedback: With this much data, chance is unlikely. Ask instead which variable drives which.

options.text: A bigger button won't change how often people tap it
options.feedback: It might. But even if everyone tapped it, nothing suggests tapping makes people watch more.

katas.hint: Who reaches for *Skip intro*: someone on episode 1 or episode 7?
katas.explanation: Bingeing makes you tap *Skip intro*, not the reverse. A bigger button might lift taps without lifting watching. To find out, show it to a random half and compare.

katas.prompt: For each correlation, which alternative explanation is most likely?

items.text: Monthly ice cream sales and drownings
Countries' chocolate consumption and Nobel prizes per person
Carrying a lighter and getting lung cancer
Students in tutoring score lower than classmates
Products with more reviews sell more
Athletes who get more massage have more injuries

katas.explanation: Heat, wealth and smoking drive both halves of the ice cream, Nobel and lighter pairs. The rest run backwards: low scores bring tutoring, sales bring reviews, injuries bring massage.

katas.title: What would make you believe it?
katas.body: Three kinds of evidence support a causal claim. **Randomization:** a coin flip decides who gets the treatment, so confounders balance out on average. **Natural experiments:** something outside anyone's control, like a lottery or a policy that stops at a border, does the assigning. **Time order:** the cause is measured before the effect, as in a group followed over years. Mechanism and dose-response add support; they don't settle it.

katas.prompt: Two analysts studied whether tutoring helps. Which plot can speak to time order?

options.text: Tutoring hours and test score, same term
options.feedback: Both were measured at once. Low scorers may have been sent to tutoring, so this plot can't tell which came first.

options.text: Tutoring hours in autumn and score change by spring

katas.hint: Which plot measured tutoring before the score?
katas.explanation: The autumn-to-spring plot measures tutoring before the score change, so the effect can't have caused the cause. It still isn't randomized: motivated students may tutor more and improve more.

katas.prompt: A product team wants to know if the onboarding tutorial raises 30-day retention. Which evidence is strongest?

options.text: Users who finished the tutorial retained at twice the rate of those who skipped
options.feedback: Self-selection. Motivated users finish tutorials *and* stick around. The tutorial may have done nothing.

options.text: Show the tutorial to a random half of new signups and compare retention
Retention rose the month the tutorial launched
options.feedback: Before-and-after is confounded by everything else that changed that month: marketing, season, bugs fixed.

options.text: In a survey, users who skipped it said they wished they hadn't
options.feedback: Opinions about the tutorial aren't evidence of its effect on retention.

katas.hint: Which option lets chance, not users, decide who gets the tutorial?
katas.explanation: Random assignment makes the two groups alike on average in motivation and everything else, so a retention gap can be credited to the tutorial.

katas.prompt: One city raises its minimum wage; the neighbouring city across the state line doesn't. Researchers compare job changes in the two. What kind of evidence is this?

options.text: A natural experiment
A randomized trial
options.feedback: Nobody flipped a coin. The policy was chosen by politicians, so it isn't randomized, though the border comparison helps.

options.text: Just another confounded correlation
options.feedback: Partly fair: the cities may differ. But the design holds shared conditions (economy, season, region) constant, which a plain correlation can't.

options.text: Reverse causation
options.feedback: Job changes didn't cause the wage law; the law came first. The worry here is confounding, not direction.

katas.explanation: A policy that stops at a border splits otherwise similar places: a natural experiment, used in well-known minimum-wage studies. Its weakness is that the two cities may still differ.

challenge.situation: Monday standup. A colleague has a hypothetical study she is excited about, and a campaign idea to go with it.

visual.alt: Priya shares a study of 10,000 adults where coffee drinkers live longer, and asks to tell customers that coffee extends life.

turns.text: Found a study of 10,000 adults: one or two cups of coffee a day, and they live longer than non-drinkers. Can we tell customers coffee extends life?

options.text: Who are the non-drinkers, though? People who quit coffee for their health would drag that group down.
options.outcome: Huh, I had not thought about who is in that group. Let me look for a study that follows healthy people over time instead.

options.text: Can we find a bigger study first? 10,000 adults feels too few to settle something like this.
options.outcome: Sure, I will look for a bigger one. Though if the two groups are different kinds of people, more of them will not change that, will it?

options.text: Go for it. 10,000 people is strong evidence, and studies that size rarely turn out wrong.
options.outcome: Perfect, I will draft the campaign today. If 10,000 people say so, legal cannot argue.

options.text: Correlation never means anything. A study like this tells us nothing about coffee.
options.outcome: So we just ignore it? Then why does anyone run studies like this at all?

challenge.explanation: The correlation could be confounded (health, income), reversed (illness reduces coffee drinking), or real. Only evidence with time order, randomization, or a natural experiment can tell which.

takeaways: Before reading a correlation as cause, name a third variable that could move both.
Ask which way the arrow points: the "effect" often drives the "cause".
Trust causal claims backed by randomization, a natural experiment, or clear time order, not by sample size.
